subject_line: The Inland Empire at the center of Mecca
email_body:
Dear Susan,

I read that you wrote Mecca for the Inland Empire community and for your students, asking why cities like Riverside can't be the centerpiece of a great book, and that its characters grew out of true stories from the region.

I'd love to ask how you decided which of those real events could carry a fictional life, and which you felt had to stay untouched.

The Author Ledger is an independent project featuring short Author Spotlights. The portrait is developed through a few written questions, which you can answer at your own pace, and the full text is shared with you for review before publication.

The Author Ledger
hook_note: Mecca (FSG, 2022) written for the Inland Empire and her UCR students, characters inspired by real regional events (UCR News release, Masters Review interview).

subject_line: Fresno, and the title of Scar and Flower
email_body:
Dear Lee,

Scar and Flower, the Northern California Book Award finalist, came out of years in which you served as Fresno Poet Laureate and went on to become California's tenth Poet Laureate, the first Asian American in that role.

I'm curious how Fresno, the city you've taught in for so long at Fresno City College, sits inside the book's pairing of scar and flower.

hook_note: Scar and Flower was a 2020 Northern California Book Award finalist; Fresno Poet Laureate 2015-17 and 10th CA Poet Laureate (FCC directory / leeherrick.com). Email seen in search result (Fresno City College faculty directory).

subject_line: Two families and one boy in Lucky Boy
email_body:
Dear Shanthi,

Lucky Boy places an undocumented young Mexican mother and an Indian-American couple in Berkeley on either side of the same child, and you live in Berkeley yourself while teaching creative writing at California College of the Arts.

I'd like to ask how writing about your own city shaped the way you balanced the two households, so that neither family became the story's villain.

subject_line: Sadie's bookstore and Houdini in True Love
email_body:
Dear Micah,

In True Love and Other Dreams of Miraculous Escape, the linked stories follow Sadie as she opens a bookstore in Santa Cruz, and then Harry Houdini turns up in "King of Chains" opposite a reporter named Albert.

I'd love to explore how an escape artist found his way into a book so rooted in a Santa Cruz bookstore, and what the linked-story form let you do that a novel would not.

subject_line: Mao's dance troupes in Forbidden City
email_body:

I'd like to ask how you turned that historical detail into a fifteen-year-old narrator with a voice of her own, and where you chose to depart from the record.

subject_line: Lou's 1930s Los Angeles in The Perishing
email_body:
Dear Natashia,

The Perishing sends Lou, a young Black woman, into 1930s Los Angeles, and on the Poured Over podcast you described researching the St. Francis Dam collapse and the 1871 massacre of Chinese laborers in the city.

I'd love to ask how your work as a criminal defense attorney shaped the way you read that buried Los Angeles history and chose what Lou would witness.

subject_line: The Bar W Ranch in The Last Rancher
email_body:
Dear Robert,

After two essay books about Dodge City and the prairie, The Last Rancher, your debut novel and a 2025 Kansas Notable Book, takes you into fiction with the Wagner family and the Bar W Ranch in southwest Kansas, where an accident brings the children home and old secrets surface.

I'd like to ask what fiction let you do with that country that Dragging Wyatt Earp and Headlights on the Prairie could not.

subject_line: Kit, Julie and We Were the Universe
email_body:
Dear Kimberly,

Congratulations on the 2025 Oregon Book Award for We Were the Universe. Kit, a young mother still half-refusing to believe her sister Julie is gone, stayed with me, and I noticed you described the novel to Texas Standard as a highly fictionalized version of your own experience of loss.

I'd like to ask how you decided where to let invention take over from what you'd lived, especially in writing Julie.

hook_note: Won 2025 Oregon Book Award (Ken Kesey Award for Fiction) for We Were the Universe; protagonist Kit grieving sister Julie; told Texas Standard the novel is a highly fictionalized version of her experience (WWeek, Texas Standard).

subject_line: From Stringing Rosaries to the poet laureate's desk
email_body:
Dear Denise,

Stringing Rosaries, your 2019 book with NDSU Press on the history of Native American boarding schools, sits beside poetry collections like His Feathers Were Chains and Thunderbird, and since 2023 you have served as North Dakota's first Native American poet laureate, with the term now extended to 2028.

I'd like to ask how the research behind Stringing Rosaries feeds your poems, and what the new book you're planning about Native students will carry forward.

The Author Ledger
hook_note: Turtle Mountain Ojibwe; ND's first Native American poet laureate (2023), term extended through June 2028; Stringing Rosaries (NDSU Press 2019); plans new book on Native students (NPR, Minot Daily News, poets.org).

subject_line: From the Akron Prize to Redmond: Something About Living

I'd like to ask how the book's attention to Palestinian history and the diaspora sits with your daily life in Redmond.

hook_note: Something About Living (Akron Poetry Prize 2022, selected by Adrian Matejka) won 2024 National Book Award and 2025 Washington State Book Award for Poetry; lives in Redmond (Seattle Magazine, Wikipedia, Viewless Wings interview).
